extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers, creative-writing students, and authors learning scene structure
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing individual scenes using Dwight V. Swain's scene–sequel model, focusing on the three-part scene (goal, conflict, disaster) and how scenes move a story forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene purpose and turning point
rubrics_metrics.description: A scene's purpose is to move the story forward and should include a climactic moment (a 'turning point'). Larger structural segments have larger turning points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nearly every scene should have a climactic moment, which is also called a 'turning point.' The bigger the structural segment, the bigger the turning point—meaning an act's turning point is going to have more ramifications than a scene-level turning point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene definition (unit of action/conflict)
rubrics_metrics.description: A scene is typically a unit of action that takes place in a single location and continuous time, and—per Swain—'a scene is a unit of conflict lived through by the character and reader.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'scene' can be ambiguous and boundaries can be blurry, but most agree a scene is one of the smallest recognized structural units in a story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of scenes vs. sequels
rubrics_metrics.description: Swain distinguishes two smallest structural units: 'scene' (where action takes place) and 'sequel' (where reaction takes place).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure your narrative by alternating action (scenes) and reaction (sequels). The sequel itself has three parts—reaction, dilemma, and decision (covered separately).

rubrics_metrics.name: Goal (scene component)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every scene should present a character's scene-level goal (something the character wants in that scene), which often ties into the overarching plot goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The goal should have significant stakes—obtaining or not obtaining it affects story direction. Almost always the audience should have a sense of the character's goal at the beginning of the scene (or it can be implied from prior context). Goals should almost always be concrete and specific; if abstract, show concrete manifestations (e.g., 'send flowers' for 'prove my love'). If a scene-level goal doesn't change outcomes or have ramifications, it may be cut.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict (scene component)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflict is the opposition that impedes the character's goal and forms the scene's rising action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The opposition may be direct or indirect, but it must stand in the way of the goal. Conflict is important because it tests the character's dedication to the goal and helps make up the plot. Use good judgment to pick the type of opposition that best suits your scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of conflict (choose appropriately)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are eight types of conflict listed that can create opposition: person vs. self, person vs. person, person vs. society, person vs. nature, person vs. god, person vs. fate, person vs. the supernatural, person vs. technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any of these can be used to create opposition—choose what best suits the scene's needs and themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Escalation of conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflict should escalate during the scene through complications and developments rather than repeating the same obstacle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have the opposition grow stronger as the scene progresses. Avoid rehashing the exact same disruption (example: don't have the phone interrupt in the exact same way repeatedly); instead introduce new complications that raise the stakes and interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disaster (scene component / outcome / hook)
rubrics_metrics.description: The disaster is the scene's outcome: an (often unanticipated) development that has significant stakes and propels the story toward a new problem or loss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Swain describes disaster as essentially 'No, and...' or 'Yes, but...' — if the character fails, add a new problem; if the character succeeds, add a new problem. The disaster should be significant (have ramifications) and ideally end the scene with a hook that makes the reader want to continue. Not every scene must end with an explicit disaster; sometimes the promise or potential of disaster is sufficient, or a positive outcome can be used to set up an imminent disappointment. Beware that ending without a new problem can make the audience 'wait' rather than anticipate the character's choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goals give audience context to measure progress
rubrics_metrics.description: A clearly established scene goal lets the audience measure whether events are progress or setback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there isn't a discernible goal, the audience can't judge advancement and may feel they are 'just watching things happen.' Make goals visible or implied so readers can track progress.
